questions.stem: A study note written in 2024 describes the BC VTS rules. What has changed for BC since then?
options: New VTS Zones Regulations repealed the old ones, in force 2026-03-31
Nothing; the 1989 zone regulations still apply unchanged
VTS became voluntary for all vessels in British Columbia
The Western zones were replaced by a single national zone
questions.explanation: Section 39 of SOR/2025-275 repeals the earlier VTS Zones Regulations, the Eastern Canada regulations and the Northern Canada regulations, and the consolidation shows the new provisions in force from 2026-03-31. VTS remains mandatory for the prescribed classes, and the Western zones are still there.

questions.stem: Which pair are the Western VTS Zones in Schedule 1?
options: Vancouver and Tofino
Victoria and Seattle
Pacific North and Pacific South
Victoria and Prince Rupert
questions.explanation: Schedule 1 lists two Western VTS Zones, Victoria and Prince Rupert. Seattle is a United States service, not a Canadian zone, and the other names are not Schedule 1 items.

questions.stem: A tug is leaving the Victoria zone for open water north of Cape Caution. Which zone covers the water just north of the Cape Caution to Cape Sutil line?
options: Victoria
No VTS zone
Prince Rupert
The Northern VTS Zone
questions.explanation: The two Western zones meet at the Cape Sutil, Mexicana Point and Cape Caution line. Victoria is inside the line; Prince Rupert covers the central and north coast beyond it. The Northern VTS Zone is an Arctic and northern zone and does not include the BC coast.

questions.stem: Under CSA s. 126, which of these may an MCTS officer do to a vessel of a prescribed class that is about to enter or is within a VTS Zone?
options: Order the vessel detained and scrapped
Grant a clearance, ask for information, set the frequency, and keep it out of an area
Change the vessel's voyage class on its certificate
Cancel or suspend the master's certificate
questions.explanation: Section 126(3) gives these four powers. The others are not powers of an MCTS officer under this section; certificates and voyage classes are dealt with under other regulations.

questions.stem: A 280 GT tug is pushing a 250 GT barge, with a combined gross tonnage of 530. Which statement is correct about the general class in s. 3?
options: Covered, as a tow with combined tonnage of 500 GT or more
Not covered, because each unit is under 300 GT
Covered only if dangerous goods are aboard
Covered only in the Prince Rupert zone
questions.explanation: Section 3(1)(b) catches a vessel engaged in towing or pushing another vessel if the combined gross tonnage is 500 GT or more. The 300 GT threshold in 3(1)(a) applies to single vessels. Carriage of dangerous goods is a separate route in 3(1)(c).

questions.stem: In the Western zones, which of these is covered by the extra 20 m class in s. 9(1)(a)?
options: A 28 m pleasure craft
A 22 m fishing vessel of 80 GT, trawling
A 19 m cargo vessel of 90 GT
A 22 m fishing vessel of 160 GT
questions.explanation: A fishing vessel is excepted only if it is under 24 m and not more than 150 GT; at 160 GT the 22 m fishing vessel is covered. The 28 m pleasure craft is under the 30 m exception, the 80 GT fishing vessel meets both parts of the exception, and the 19 m vessel is under 20 m.

questions.stem: A 31 m private motor yacht (a pleasure craft) and a 25 m pleasure craft cruise the Strait of Georgia. Which are covered by the Western add-on class?
options: Both, as both are over 20 m
Neither, as both are pleasure craft
Only the 31 m yacht
Only the 25 m craft
questions.explanation: Section 9(1)(a) covers a vessel of 20 m or more other than a pleasure craft under 30 m. At 31 m the yacht is covered; at 25 m the pleasure craft falls within the exception.

questions.stem: A 15 m tug pushes a log boom whose length is 30 m on open water in the Strait of Georgia. Under s. 9(1)(b), is she covered?
options: No, because she is under 20 m in length
Yes, because the tow is 20 m or more
Only if the boom is within a log booming ground
Only if the boom contains dangerous goods
questions.explanation: Section 9(1)(b) covers a vessel towing or pushing another vessel or an object (other than fishing gear) if the combined length is 45 m or more or the length of what is towed or pushed is 20 m or more. A tow wholly within a log booming ground is excluded, but this one is on open water.

questions.stem: Which vessels must file the 24-hour sailing plan on entering a VTS Zone from outside Canadian waters?
options: The general class in s. 3, by tonnage, tow size or cargo
Every vessel covered by any part of the Regulations
Only vessels carrying passengers for hire
Only vessels of 20 m or more in length
questions.explanation: Section 10 sets the 24-hour sailing plan and it sits with the general class; the Western add-on class gets ss. 11 to 15 only. If the voyage from the last port is under 24 hours, the plan goes in as soon as feasible before entering.

questions.stem: A covered 20 m vessel is about to leave a berth in the Victoria zone. When is the sailing plan due, and when is the position report due?
options: Sailing plan 5 minutes after leaving; position report at the next buoy
Both 24 hours before leaving the berth
Sailing plan on arrival; position report at 1600 UTC
Plan at least 15 minutes before; position report just before leaving
questions.explanation: Section 11(c) requires the sailing plan at least 15 minutes before departing a berth in a zone, and s. 12(c) requires the position report immediately before departure. The 1600 UTC daily report belongs to the Northern zone (s. 33).

questions.stem: A vessel has just crossed Active Pass and is passing a calling-in point named in RAMN Part 3 in the Victoria zone. What report does s. 12 require?
options: A deviation report only, if the plan changed
A final report to the Victoria centre
A position report on arriving at the point
No report, because calling-in points are optional
questions.explanation: Section 12(a) requires a position report on arrival at each calling-in point. A final report is made on arrival at a berth or immediately before leaving the zone (s. 13). A deviation report follows a significant change in earlier information (s. 15).

questions.stem: A covered vessel is about to leave the Victoria zone and enter the Prince Rupert zone, with no stop between. When is the final report due?
options: Immediately before leaving Victoria, as the Regulations always require
Not required, because the vessel enters another VTS zone
Within 30 days, by letter to the Coast Guard
At the next calling-in point in the new zone
questions.explanation: Section 13(b) requires a final report immediately before the vessel leaves a zone, except if it enters any other VTS zone. A final report is still made on arrival at a berth (s. 13(a)).

questions.stem: Which of these must be reported to MCTS as an "other report" under s. 14 once the master is aware of it?
options: A defect in the vessel's steering system
A change of crew at the next port
A routine fuel top-up at the berth
The tidal height at the berth
questions.explanation: Section 14(d) covers a defect in the hull, main propulsion, steering, anchor or any equipment required under the Navigation Safety Regulations, 2020. The list also includes fire, collision, grounding, unforeseen bottom contact, cargo shifting, a pollutant in the water, hazardous ice or weather and a damaged aid to navigation.

questions.stem: Halfway through a passage in a VTS zone, a vessel changes its destination and ETA from what it reported earlier. What report follows?
options: No report is needed if the vessel is still inside the zone
A new 24-hour sailing plan before carrying on
A final report immediately, then a new sailing plan
A deviation report as soon as feasible
questions.explanation: Section 15 requires a deviation report containing updated information as soon as feasible after the master becomes aware of a significant change in the information in a report. The 24-hour plan is only for entering from outside Canadian waters.

questions.stem: A covered vessel inside the Victoria zone loses its VHF to an equipment failure and the vessel is not in a port or anchorage where it can be repaired. What does CSA s. 126(6) require?
options: Proceed on the planned route at normal speed and report on arrival in port
Stop in the channel and wait for the radio to be fixed
Go to the nearest safe port or anchorage on its route and stay there
Drift until a Coast Guard vessel arrives on scene
questions.explanation: Where the inability to communicate is due to equipment failure on the vessel and it is not in a port or anchorage where the equipment can be repaired, the vessel must go to the nearest reasonably safe port or anchorage on its route when it is safe to do so and stay there. If the problem is only that contact cannot be made (no equipment failure), the vessel may proceed but must keep trying.

questions.stem: A vessel cannot get a clearance because MCTS does not answer, and there is no equipment failure on the vessel. What is the position under s. 126(4) and (5)?
options: It must anchor immediately until MCTS replies
It may proceed, but must keep trying to communicate and get a clearance
It must return to its berth and wait for a clearance
It may proceed and need not try to call again
questions.explanation: Section 126(4) permits the vessel to proceed on its route; s. 126(5) requires all reasonable measures to communicate as soon as possible and a clearance once communication is established. The stay-in-port rule in subsection (6) applies only where the cause is equipment failure on the vessel.

questions.stem: Inside the Victoria traffic zone, which VHF channel does the NSR require for the listening watch and navigation safety calls?
options: The zone's assigned VHF channel, set by Notices to Mariners or law
Channel 16, always, in every zone
Channel 13, as on the Great Lakes
Channel 6, the ship-to-ship channel
questions.explanation: Schedule 4 item 2 of the Navigation Safety Regulations, 2020 puts a vessel in waters under Canadian jurisdiction (outside the Great Lakes) on Channel 16 outside a traffic zone and on the appropriate VHF channel inside one. A vessel that is reporting to a traffic centre need not make the departure and dredge-approach navigation safety calls.

questions.stem: You are headed out of Haro Strait into the Strait of Georgia in the Victoria zone. According to the 2026 RAMN extract used for this lesson, which channel does Victoria Traffic use for the sector covering Haro Strait, Boundary Pass and the Strait of Georgia?
options: Channel 5A
Channel 16
Channel 74
Channel 11
questions.explanation: RAMN Part 3 (2026) lists Victoria Traffic on Channel 11 for that sector, while Prince Rupert Traffic works the west coast of Vancouver Island on Channel 74. These channels come from a summary of the RAMN page, so check the current published table before relying on them.
